title: Granular kernel selection and multi-dim shard coordinator (draft)
content:
Purpose and context:

This note describes an approach to reduce tail latency and throughput variance for large-model inference on multi-GPU nodes by combining: (1) a lightweight per-request kernel scoring and selection layer (granular kernel selection) and (2) a multi-dimensional shard coordinator that makes soft partitioning decisions across tensor/pipeline parallel stages. The goal is an operationally simple runtime hook that adapts to heterogeneous model kernels, varying sequence lengths, and noisy NCCL behavior without performing heavy global rebalancing.

Why a new approach?

Observed failure modes in production (summary):
- High tail latency from mismatched kernel choices for short-vs-long sequences (some kernels are optimized for short prefixes, others for long context).
- NCCL collective stalls when mixed-size all-reduce patterns collide on oversubscribed PCIe/NIC paths.
- Aggressive static sharding exposes QoS fragility: a single noisy tenant or spike can cause cascading backpressure in downstream stages.
- KV cache coherency overhead when shards are frequently remapped or when activations are partially mirrored.

Design constraints and non-goals:
- Must be implementable as a runtime layer that can be toggled per-node without model recompilation.
- Avoid heavy synchronous resharding that would block inference lanes for >100ms.
- Keep changes local to the serving runtime and NCCL orchestration hooks; no changes required in user prompts or model graphs.
- Non-goal: full physical re-sharding of weights at runtime (that is out-of-scope for this doc).

High-level idea:

1) Per-request kernel scoring: for each incoming request we compute a small feature vector (sequence length, token distribution roughness, past-kv-hit-rate, priority tier) and run a fast scoring function that biases kernel selection among candidate execution kernels (e.g., fused-attn-int8, block-sparse, or fallback float16). The scoring function is a weighted linear model with online-updatable weights derived from recent microbenchmarks and SLO feedback.

2) Soft partitioning shard coordinator: instead of absolute assignment of layers -> GPUs, we maintain soft ownership probabilities for each shard. At scheduling time we pick the concrete placement by sampling with constraints (local memory budget, NCCL link load estimate, tenant affinity). This allows quick re-routing of new requests away from congested links without moving state.

3) Bandwidth-aware NCCL pacing: the coordinator monitors per-link utilization and injects micro-scheduling pauses (5-15ms) and adaptive chunking into all-reduce/all-gather primitives to avoid synchronized peaks.

4) Versioned KV deltas: KV cache coherence is handled by a lightweight versioned-delta protocol. When a request is routed to a non-primary shard, we fetch only missing KV deltas; deltas are small and piggybacked on existing collectives where possible.

Detailed components:

A. Kernel scoring module (KS):
- Inputs: seq_len, prefix_len, expected output length, kv_hit_rate_estimate (0..1), model_variant_tags, priority
- Output: ordered list of (kernel_id, score) candidate kernels
- Implementation notes: keep model small (<= 64 B-parameters) and deterministic. Start with linear model: score = w0 + w1*log(seq_len) + w2*kv_hit + w3*priority_weight + sum(tag_weights).
- Online update: after each request record observed latency/cost and update weights via SGD with small learning rate. Use EMA-slots to avoid catastrophic drift.

B. Multi-dim shard coordinator (MSC):
- State: for each shard S, maintain: owner_set (GPUs with local weights), soft_weights (probabilities), last_update_ts, link_stress_estimate.
- Scheduling logic: on request arrival, compute candidate shards satisfying memory/residency constraints and sample an owner according to soft_weights but reweighted by current link_stress_estimate (prefers lower stress). If a requested owner lacks a needed KV version, trigger a delta fetch.
- Soft reassignment policy: periodically (1s) decay soft_weights toward steady state observed utilization; on sustained overload (>3s), amplify alternative owners. This avoids immediate flip-flopping.

C. NCCL pacing and chunking:
- Monitor metrics: per-collective bandwidth, average queue depth at NIC, observed collective latency per size bucket.
- Default policy: for collectives larger than 16MB, split into adaptive chunks where chunk_size = clamp(8MB * (1 - nic_util), 2MB, 16MB). Insert small inter-chunk gaps (5ms) when peer count > 8 to reduce synchronized contention on shared NICs.
- For heterogeneous link speeds (NVLink + PCIe mix), prefer route-favoring: place shards so that the heaviest collectives are NVLink-local if possible (MSC uses link cost model).

D. KV cache delta protocol:
- Each shard maintains monotonic version counters for shard-local KV prefixes.
- When a request is scheduled to a GPU that does not have the latest version, the runtime issues a delta-fetch RPC to a local KV-coordinator (not the central control plane) that serves versioned deltas. Deltas are compressed and may be applied incrementally.
- In the common case (hot prefixes), the coordinator will maintain a small replica set so delta-fetch is one-hop local.

Failure handling and fallbacks:
- If a chosen kernel fails (OOM or internal assert) fallback to next kernel in KS list. Fallbacks should record telemetry and trigger weight decay for the failed kernel.
- If delta-fetch latency exceeds threshold (50ms), MSC should re-sample an alternative owner that has the needed version or route to a replicated owner.
- If NCCL pacing indicates persistent tail spikes (>5th percentile > SLA*1.5), increase chunking aggressiveness and optionally shift preferred owners away from the saturated NIC.

Simulations and synthetic tests (plan):
- Microbench harness that replays production traces with mixed sequence lengths and priority tiers. Goals: verify 99.9th latency delta, increased throughput, and reduced NCCL stall counts.
- Test scenarios: single noisy tenant with short bursts; balanced all-tenants; sudden KV-population shifts (cold-start prefixes); degraded link (simulate NIC 50% slower).
- Metrics to capture: per-request kernel success rate, kernel selection latency overhead, number of delta-fetches per request, NCCL stall count, 99th/99.9th latency, cost per token estimate.

Rollout plan (canary -> fleet):
- Stage 0: unit tests & microbench harness (local).
- Stage 1: canary on dedicated pool with non-critical models (50 GPUs). Observe telemetry for 24h.
- Stage 2: controlled A/B with production traffic for low-priority tier, 72h.
- Stage 3: enable adaptive online updates to KS weights for low-priority only, validate stability.
- Stage 4: open to all traffic if no regressions.

Operational considerations:
- Telemetry: record kernel_id, score_vector, chosen_owner, link_stress_at_schedule, delta_fetch_time, fallback_count. Keep these traces for 7 days at high resolution and 90 days as aggregates.
- Debugging tools: per-GPU timeline view showing kernel switches, collectives, and delta RPCs (helpful for reproducing tail events).
- Controls: admin knobs to disable KS online learning, force kernel, or pin shards to owners for debugging.

Open questions / risks:
- How to prevent KS learning from optimizing for adversarial request patterns (malicious tenants crafting prompts to force expensive kernels)? Consider clipping weight updates and per-tenant regularization.
- Soft partitioning reduces physical migration but still requires careful memory accounting when many owners are eligible. Need eviction heuristics for shadow replicas.
- The delta protocol adds network hops; must ensure delta size stays small via compression and prefix coalescing.

Next steps / TODOs:
- Implement kernel-scoring prototype and run synthetic short/long mix. (owner, Priya)
- Add MSC simulated scheduler in our existing scheduler simulator and run link-degradation tests. (Marco)
- Build per-link NIC/PCIe stress monitor and expose as runtime metric. (Elena)
- Draft design for delta RPC (serialization, compression). (Roberto)

Appendix: quick pseudocode for scheduling path

function schedule_request(req):
  features = extract_features(req)
  candidates = KS.score_candidates(features)  # ordered list
  for kernel in candidates:
    if kernel_compatible_with_node(kernel):
      owner = MSC.choose_owner(req, kernel)
      if owner.has_kv_version(req.kv_version):
        return submit_to_owner(owner, kernel, req)
      else:
        delta_ok = fetch_delta_with_timeout(owner, req.kv_version, 50ms)
        if delta_ok:
          return submit_to_owner(owner, kernel, req)
  # fallbacks: try other kernels, or route to fallback fleet
  return submit_to_fallback(req)
End of draft.

If this approach looks promising I can split into separate PRDs: one focused on kernel scoring (fast wins) and one on MSC + delta protocol (more invasive). Feedback welcome, especially on tuning knobs for NCCL chunking and acceptable delta-fetch latencies.
